title: Fates of Exact Finite-$N$ First-Order Transitions: Coherent Suppression versus Spectral-Collapse Termination
authors: Jiong Li, Li-Wei Duan, Qing-Hu Chen, Hai-Qing Lin
abstract: Symmetry-protected ground-state crossings can produce exact first-order transitions (FOTs) even at finite $N$, in contrast to continuous transitions governed by soft-mode criticality. We establish exact Juddian ground-state crossings for arbitrary finite $N$ in the one- and two-photon anisotropic Dicke models and identify a common two-channel structure: the eigenvalues of the coupling matrix set the local normal-state instability thresholds, whereas its determinant fixes the exact crossing. Despite this common structure, the resulting FOTs have distinct fates determined by the bosonic response. In the one-photon model, the overlap between coherent Juddian branches vanishes in the thermodynamic or infinite frequency-ratio limits, asymptotically suppressing the FOT cusp. In the two-photon model, squeezed Juddian states lose normalizability at spectral collapse, thereby terminating the physical FOT line at finite $N$. Although the cusp strength tends to zero as the endpoint is approached, the terminating FOT retains a collective spectral signature: the different-parity gap is predicted to close with an $N$-dependent exponent $μ_N=(2N+3)/4$, one greater than the cusp termination exponent. By contrast, the same-parity soft mode retains $N$-independent square-root scaling and governs the critical response. Thus spectral collapse can terminate an exact finite-$N$ FOT while preserving its collective imprint in the parity-resolved spectrum.
summary: This theoretical paper investigates how first-order quantum phase transitions behave at finite particle numbers in Dicke-type models. It distinguishes between two fates: asymptotic suppression (one-photon) and termination at a finite-coupling boundary due to spectral collapse (two-photon). The key finding is that even when the transition terminates, a distinct, measurable collective spectral signature persists.
main_problem: The paper compares the physical fates of exact first-order quantum phase transitions (FOTs) occurring at finite particle number ($N$) in anisotropic Dicke models, contrasting asymptotic suppression with termination due to spectral collapse.
main_result: In the one-photon case, the FOT cusp strength vanishes asymptotically, while in the two-photon case, the FOT terminates at a finite-coupling boundary, leaving a distinct, $N$-dependent collective spectral signature.
method: The analysis uses Juddian solutions to characterize the crossing points and employs perturbation theory, scaling arguments, and gap analysis near the critical/collapse endpoints.
model_or_system: The study focuses on anisotropic Dicke Models (ADMs) in one-photon and two-photon regimes, involving coupling to a single bosonic mode and exhibiting symmetry-protected ground-state crossings.
key_observables: FOT cusp strength ($J^{(k)}_X$), different-parity gap ($\epsilon_{dp}$), same-parity soft-mode gap ($\epsilon_{sp}$), and Quantum Fisher Information ($F_Q$).
important_parameters: Finite particle number $N$, coupling constants ($g_J$), and the spectral collapse boundary defined by $g_c$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of exact Juddian ground-state doublets for arbitrary finite $N$ and relies on specific scaling estimates for various quantum overlaps and gaps.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate low-energy spectra showing the FOT crossing relative to instability thresholds, and plot the scaling of parity-resolved gaps ($\epsilon_{dp}$ vs $\epsilon_{sp}$) and QFI near the collapse endpoint.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the common structure of the crossing via the coupling matrix determinant, then analyzes the distinct bosonic responses in the one-photon (asymptotic suppression) and two-photon (spectral collapse) models, culminating in a detailed comparison of gap scaling exponents.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed, quantitative comparison of how different physical mechanisms (thermodynamic vs. finite-size effects) govern the disappearance or modification of quantum critical points, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum phase transitions in cavity QED or superconducting circuits.
